segments.english: 4) The authority of our rabbis, the masters of the new Kabbalah, shall not be greater than the authority of the Great Beit Din who sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, and their grasp is no greater than the grasp of the Great Sanhedrin! And yet the Torah said that if they erred and ruled to permit the forbidden, or sinned inadvertently in idolatry, etc. We have learned from the Torah and from our rabbis, in the tractate Horayot, that the Great Beit Din can err and rule a permission in some particular case of idolatry. For man is formed of clay, whether great or small, and is prone to err; therefore the Torah commanded: "If a matter is too hard for you in judgment, etc. Then arise and go up to the place that the LORD your God will choose," in order to lessen the error. How is it not unavoidable that even the Great Beit Din should err. For it is said in the Torah, "and the matter was hidden from the eyes of the assembly. And it shall be, if from the eyes of the congregation it was done in error." And according to the shortness of our understanding, when we see the great difference between our early rabbis, and how was their faith in the matter of divinity and the unity of the Name, may He be blessed, according to the holy Torah, as explained by Rabbeinu Bachya, the author of Chovot ha-Levavot, and Rabbi Yehuda Halevi in the Kuzari and in his prayers, and Rabbi Saadia Gaon in the Emunot ve-De'ot, and the Rambam in his work, and in his commentary on the Mishnah, and in the Moreh Nevukhim. And the Roke'ach in the Gate of Unity, and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol, and Rabbi Yosef Albo in the Sefer ha-Ikkarim, and Rabbi Meir Aldabi in the Shvilei Emunah. And many others, and likewise the complete ones. And how is it now in the books of our later rabbis, according to the new Kabbalah, which runs from the start of the sixth millennium with cords of falsehood until it became in our time as with cart-ropes, and they believed in many gods. And that the principal point in them, to which all our worship and blessings are directed, is the last partzuf in Emanation, called (quick to anger) Ze'ir Anpin.

grammar: ולא יהא כח ... גדול מכח: a negated future (יהא) with a comparison; the English keeps the repeated 'the authority of' so that the comparison is plain.
איך אינו נמנע שלא יטעו: a rhetorical question in form with a full stop in the Hebrew; the English keeps it as a question of argument ('How is it not unavoidable...').
Three Torah passages are cited: Deut 17:8 (quoted, with וכו' as the author's truncation sign), Lev 4:13 and Num 15:24 (introduced by שהרי נאמר בתורה and continued by והיה).
The long period ולפי קוצר דעתינו ... is divided at 'when we see' and 'how was their faith'; no clause is dropped and the order of the list of authors is kept.
segments.note: Plain sentences follow the Hebrew full stops. The Torah quotations take double quotation marks; the author's וכו' is kept as 'etc.'. The list of authors is elliptical in the Hebrew after the full stop at הנבוכים, and the English keeps that ellipsis.
apparatus: Base text: Wikisource; not yet collated with the 1931 scan (open question 2), so the English is the base text as it stands.
Printed list marker ד) (the fourth item) opens the paragraph; the next paragraph opens ה) (the fifth item).
Deut 17:8, quoted with 'etc.' marking the author's omission (וכו').
Lev 4:13, quoted: ונעלם דבר מעיני הקהל.
Num 15:24, quoted: והיה אם מעיני העדה נעשתה לשגגה.
Isa 5:18, embedded allusion (no quotation marks): בחבלי השוא and כעבות העגלה.
Prov 14:17, for the author's קצר אפים, set against ארך אפים in Exod 34:6.
context: The Chamber of Hewn Stone (lishkat ha-gazit): the chamber in the Temple where the Great Court sat, as the author's words place it. The Hebrew gives no further detail.

segments.english: 5) And this new faith is very far from the way of our holy Torah, written and oral. Therefore we separated ourselves from it, and we clung to the words of our rabbis of blessed memory, the masters of the Mishnah and the Talmud, Bavli and Yerushalmi, and the decisors, and the midrashim of our famous rabbis, Midrash Rabbah and Tanchuma and Yalkut Shimoni, and the great Midrash found in Yemen in manuscript, and Nur al-Salam, and the like. Also, the remnant of the books of our forebears, the sages of Yemen, we find and see that they adhere to the words of the great ones mentioned above and to their opinions. And as you see that we separated from the new Kabbalah, your anger burned against us, and in haughtiness of spirit you ascribed to us arrogant falsehood. And we asked you to teach us the way: how would the words of our rabbis, the new Kabbalists, agree with the words of our early rabbis mentioned above, and with the words of the Tannaim and the Amoraim. And your answer to us was in the manner of deception and quarrels.

grammar: The paragraph is a chain of first-person plural past acts (פירשנו, ודבקנו, שאלנו); the reply of the other side is in the perfect (והיתה) and is given as a report.
ושאלנו אתכם ... איך יסכימו: the question is indirect (איך with the imperfect) and carries a full stop; the English keeps it as a report, 'how would ... agree'.
ברמות רוחא is an Aramaic idiom for arrogance and is translated by its sense; the literal is in the phrase literal.
segments.note: The list of sources is kept in the order the author gives it. The Midrash ha-Gadol and Nur al-Salam are named only by their description and title in the Hebrew.
